I've found the number one obstacle to discussing privacy with people is their expectation of an all-or-nothing proposition. You have to break privacy down into manageable bites.

  • There's system security - such as your operating system and wireless keyboard. Make sure your security updates are completed and stuff...
  • There's communication security - use a secure email client that supports encryption; use a secure texting app like Signal; use secure, encrypted file transfer protocols and services...
  • Internet browsing security - against tracking and propaganda and censorship.

Now on top of all that, there are different groups you want to be protected from:

  • Government and security agencies such as NSA and FBI
  • ISP's and government censorship
  • Commercial interests such as copyright organizations that seek to corrupt our laws and government and bleed us dry like vampires
  • Random other people and criminals.

Now you can keep your ISP and corporations and even law enforcement and most government interest out of your business easily. You can configure your browser, email, SMS, and VPN to become impenetrable to them for all practical purposes; and you can encrypt your hard drives and phone if you really care that much. There are some people who would have the know-how to break into some of your data, but without a compelling reason to, they will not.

Government security agencies, on the other hand, are another matter completely. Not even the dark web over Tor is really safe. You must assume that they are listening, and if motivated enough, can find out who you are. Much of these precautions will help in keeping your data private from these agencies, but my confidence in them is much lower.

All of the proported issues arising from not having net neutrality have nothing to do with net neutrality. Things like ISPs being able to strangle one service while promoting another, they can do that already. There were other more ridiculous and alarmist metaphors being thrown around, like ISPs deliberately ruining your driveway then charging you extra, but they're so far out of whack with what net neutrality actually is that I'm pretty sure they can safely be dismissed as propaganda.

Meanwhile there are actual advantages to doing away with net neutrality to do with efficient use of network resources and price signals. Right now we pay for contracts based on a bandwidth cap. This means that at slack times on the network our speed is artificially throttled and at peak times we don't even get what we pay for. Imagine only being able to drive at 30mph on an open motorway because your contract says so. Or paying for a 120mph contract which you almost never get to use because you're stuck in rush hour traffic all day.

A much better system would be to pay for priority. So at peak times, the customers with the most urgent business are prioritised (and pay for the privilege), whereas less important traffic is assigned less throughput. Equally, at slack times, you can use all the bandwidth there is because everyone else is asleep. So gamers, research projects transferring large amounts of data, torrenters etc. can take advantage of the underused network at relatively low prices.

That system is much more efficient because it makes good use of price signals, but it's not permitted under net neutrality. Bottom line is that there's no good reason not to, and all the arguments against it are actually complaining about the lack of competition. Something adding more regulation can't solve.
